To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the k-vote rules are generically stable if and only if k=2; (ii) the two-location divergent equilibriums are the most common ones, are robust to free entry and to candidates’ uncertainty about voters’ preferences, and are the only ones which exist for a non-degeneracy class of distributions when (k=2) - a class which includes all log- concave distributions.
the plurality rule is the only k-vote rule that is unstable in equilibrium, and that two-location equilibria are stable and robust to free-entry for k = 2.
the plurality rule generically fails to yield stability and that the two-vote rule generically yields stability and, moreover, has some attractive features.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the Hotelling- Down model under k-vote rules and, in doing so, it sheds light on the relationship between the stability of equilibria and the electoral rules.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the k=2 rule is the only rule which is both stable and robust in electoral competition, and that the plurality rule is the only one which is not.
the two-vote rule is the unique k-voting rule which is stable in electoral competition and, in addition, it admits two-location equilibria with desirable properties.
k=2 is the best rule to be considered for electoral competition.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the plurality rule is the worst k-vote rule for electoral competition in the sense that it generically fails to have a stable equilibrium, and that, among all k-vote rules, the two-vote rule is the best in the sense that its equilibria have a rich and robust structure.
the k = 2-vote rule is a very appealing alternative to plurality voting in terms of both existence of an equilibrium and its features.
, in contrast to the plurality rule, the two-vote rule is the most stable voting rule in electoral competition.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the plurality rule is a very special case of k-vote rule and that the latter may be more appealing than the former in terms of its stability properties.
the plurality rule (and, more generally, single-vote rules) should be abandoned as a voting mechanism in the Hotelling- Down model.
multiple votes can be an effective tool for enhancing the stability of electoral competition.
